### Remarks

This section introduced the random network FFRCISTG (RNFFRCISTG), in which the network is generated by the causal model, and the bipartite random network FFRCISTG (BRNFFRCISTG), in which people link only to places and each person's row of the adjacency matrix is a variable of their own unit.

Estimation can be straightforward. Under single-world independence and the homogeneity assumptions, the entries of each covariate are independent given what precedes them and share a common conditional law, a kernel, given their own history and network values, so person-level models can be fitted with standard methods and combined through the g-formula. The law of a whole graph generator, by contrast, is observed once and cannot be estimated. Effects of regimes that leave the network as it was realized need only the kernels; regimes that change the network, as vaccination drives do in Example 3, need the row kernel as well, which local row formation makes estimable ([Nonparametric estimation](#sec-est-bipartite-random-networks)).

Sampling is harder. A random network NPSEM describes a study vector of fixed size, and adding a person to the study yields a different model, whose realizations are incompatible with the former. The route around this runs through the units rather than the model: no contagion and single-world independence reduce the law to a few conditional laws shared by all units, so the units studied may be regarded as part of a larger population governed by the same laws, as i.i.d. observations are regarded as draws from an infinite one, and those laws become the targets of inference. In a network of people, sampling also induces measurement error in the network: each included person's network values are computed only from those of their contacts who were also sampled.

Bipartiteness mitigates this problem but does not eliminate it. Because people link only to places, each person's row of the adjacency matrix belongs to their own observational unit, and when all places are fully ascertained and people are sampled, each included person's row is well measured. The place values those rows point to need not be. A value the place generates itself, such as its decision to run a vaccination drive, is measured directly, even when people's measurements are among its inputs. A value aggregated over sampled people, such as the proportion vaccinated among a place's sampled visitors, is a noisy proxy for the true value, and it is this mismeasured value that enters people's structural equations.

In the next section, we show how a model of this form can be used to coordinate a real outbreak response—whether through **targeted vaccination**, **screening referral**, or **intensified information dissemination**—demonstrating how network-based causal models can inform efficient and equitable public health intervention.
